---
name: 3d-jutsu
title: Higgsfield 3D Jutsu
description: Build, edit, render and export hosted 3D scenes with the scene_builder_3d tools, free to build with nothing to rent or install. Use for 3D scene, room, set, prop layout, camera, lighting or animation work in a 3D Jutsu project.
---

# Higgsfield 3D Jutsu

3D Jutsu is a hosted, revision-controlled 3D scene. You build and edit it by running Python (`bpy`) through the `scene_builder_3d_*` tools; nothing is installed on the user's computer. Talk to the user about their scene, project, render and export, not about containers or the runner.

## Pick the route first

A 3D scene can be built in three places:

- This hosted scene: free to build. Nothing to rent or install, and building, editing and rendering spend no credits; only an AI image or video made from a render does. The simple default.
- Blender Studio: the prosumer option. A rented GPU box running full Blender that the user opens in the browser, for heavier or professional work, their own files and generated meshes. The GPU is billed in credits by the second for as long as the box runs.
- The Blender on the user's own computer (`/scene-builder`): free, needs a one-time setup.
  Settle the route before creating a project, renting anything or spending credits.

Go without asking only when the user already chose the route:

- They typed `/3d-jutsu`, asked for a hosted 3D Jutsu scene, or are continuing a 3D Jutsu project: continue here.
- They name Blender Studio, or a Blender Studio box is already in use in this conversation: this is not the route. Load `get_preset_instructions` with `{"preset":"/gpu"}` and work in that Blender. Do not create a hosted project for it.
- They selected `/scene-builder` or their own local Blender: that route keeps the work. Offer this one only as an alternative, never silently.

In every other case ask once which route they want, before anything else. This covers a 3D scene with no route named, new views of a supplied location, and "in Blender" without saying which Blender.

- Ask with this client's question tool when it has one, else in one short message.
- Offer only the routes you have tools for: this one needs `scene_builder_3d_*`, Blender Studio needs `gpu_rent` with `kind: blender_studio`. When only one route is left, say which and continue without asking.
- Describe each option by what the user gets and what it costs, and put your recommendation first. For example: "a hosted 3D scene: free to build, nothing to rent or install", "Blender Studio: full Blender in the browser for heavier, pro work, the GPU is billed by the second", "the Blender on your computer: free, needs a one-time setup". Say which is free and which costs credits every time you offer them.
- The answer holds for the rest of the conversation: do not ask again for later 3D requests.

Two more rules, whatever the route:

- One standalone 3D model of an object from an image, with no scene around it, is not a scene: use image-to-3D generation.
- One specific subject from a reference image (a character, a creature, a product) inside a scene: ask once whether to generate it from the image (costs credits, close likeness, harder to edit) or model it from simple shapes (no generation cost, simpler, editable). This version imports catalog assets only, so a generated or uploaded mesh cannot enter a hosted scene: say so, and offer a catalog asset, a build from simple shapes here, or Blender Studio. Never wrap a picture around a mesh as its texture in place of modelling and materials.

If no `scene_builder_3d_*` tools are available on this connector, say that hosted 3D Jutsu is not available here.

## Reconstruct a location from an image

Once the route is settled as this hosted scene, for new views of the same supplied location load
`/3d-jutsu/references/location-new-angles` with `get_preset_instructions` before
construction or appearance generation. It owns source-camera calibration, hidden
layout, shot acceptance, generation approval and bounded corrections. Image critique
alone does not authorize scene work. Keep the scene workflow below for other 3D tasks.

## Choose the project

Every project-scoped tool takes an explicit `projectId`; no call sets an active project.

- An existing scene: `scene_builder_3d_list_projects`, match the user's named project, and ask when the match is ambiguous.
- A new scene: `scene_builder_3d_create_project` once. If its response is uncertain, list projects before retrying; another create can make a duplicate.
- An authorized project with `exists: false` is a valid empty scene at revision 0, not an error.

## The loop

Two numbers guard every write: `revision` (the committed version) and `sceneSequence` (the settled scene state your code was written against).

1. `scene_builder_3d_get_project` for the current revision, scene sequence and any active operation.
2. `scene_builder_3d_query_python` to inspect names, dimensions, transforms, materials, cameras, lights and RNA before editing. Queries commit nothing; use them freely. Never guess a name, unit or API.
3. Pick a stable, descriptive `operationId` such as `add-key-light-01`. It is an idempotency key: reuse it only to retry the identical code against identical guards.
4. `scene_builder_3d_run_python` with the query's `revisionBefore` as `revision` and `sceneSequenceAfter` as `expectedSceneSequence`.
5. One mutation at a time per project, imports included. If an operation is still active, poll `scene_builder_3d_get_operation` with the same IDs. Only `succeeded`, `failed`, `timed_out` and `expired` are terminal.
6. On success, `revisionAfter` is the new head.
7. On a stale-state conflict, do not replay the code. Re-query, work out what changed, and regenerate the edit with fresh guards and a new operation ID.

Read the operation's `error.code`, `error.retryable` and any `error.retryAdvice` before retrying:

- Python exception: read the message and `output.stderrTail`, fix the code.
- `EXECUTION_TIMEOUT`: nothing was committed. Retry only with cheaper or split work.
- `CONTAINER_UNAVAILABLE` or another retryable transient error: the runtime was not free and nothing was committed. Resubmit the same code under a new operation ID against the same unchanged guards; do not rewrite working code or report it as a scene failure.

## The runtime

- `bpy` API 5.2, headless. `scene.render.engine` accepts only `BLENDER_EEVEE`, `BLENDER_WORKBENCH` and `CYCLES`; there is no `BLENDER_EEVEE_NEXT`.
- Removed APIs that raise: `SceneEEVEE.use_bloom`, `Mesh.use_auto_smooth` (use `shade_smooth()` or a Smooth by Angle modifier), `RenderSettings.tile_x`/`tile_y`, pre-AgX looks. `view_settings.look` takes values such as `'AgX - High Contrast'`. When unsure, query the RNA enum or `dir()` the struct first.
- Execution has a service-configured deadline (currently about five minutes per operation) and code is capped at 256 KiB. Renders are the expensive part: keep resolution and samples small and split large builds into coherent mutations.
- The runtime has no network access. Do not fetch URLs, read files from elsewhere, or embed model or image bytes in Python.
- Each operation starts from the settled scene, not from your previous operation's selection. Look objects up by name, such as `bpy.data.objects["HERO_robot"]`.
- Assign a concise JSON-serializable value to `result`: the names, counts and dimensions you need next, not a dump of scene state.

## Publish renders

`artifacts` is the only way a file leaves an operation:

```python
target = artifacts.file(name="preview.png", media_type="image/png")
scene.render.filepath = str(target.path)
scene.render.image_settings.media_type = "IMAGE"  # set before file_format
scene.render.image_settings.file_format = "PNG"
bpy.ops.render.render(write_still=True)
target.publish()  # unpublished files are discarded
```

At most eight `image/png`, `image/jpeg` or `video/mp4` files per operation. Names are 1-64 characters of letters, digits, `.`, `_` or `-`, starting with a letter or digit. A mismatched media type, missing file or oversize file fails the whole operation. For video set `media_type = "VIDEO"`, then `file_format = "FFMPEG"`, `ffmpeg.format = "MPEG4"`, `ffmpeg.codec = "H264"`.

Retrieve published files with `scene_builder_3d_get_artifact`, passing the operation ID for a query artifact or the revision for a committed one. Inspect the image with this client's image capability. If you cannot view it, say which visual checks remain unverified.

## Bring in models

Models enter only through `scene_builder_3d_search_assets` then `scene_builder_3d_import_asset`, copying the search result's `importArguments` (including `catalogSearch`). This version imports curated catalog assets only; it cannot import a user's own file. Each import is one tracked object. Adjust it afterwards with a mutation rather than importing again. If `settled` is false, poll `scene_builder_3d_get_project` until `appliedSceneSequence` reaches `targetSceneSequence`. If an import fails, report it; never fall back to Python downloads or base64.

## Build a scene, not a script

A scene is an editable visual system at metre scale, judged from its delivery camera. For anything beyond one object, decide the deliverable, the hero, midground and background roles and their fidelity, the camera, and the light motivation before building. Name objects by role (`HERO_robot`, `ENV_floor`, `CAM_main`, `LGT_key`) and keep semantic parts, modifiers and materials editable.

The first blockout mutation places the delivery camera and a working light rig: modest world ambient, one motivated key (`LGT_key`), one soft fill. Use Sun, Spot or Point lights: the scene view and GLB export drop Area lights. Then work coarse to fine and do not polish past a failed gate: silhouette, proportion (verify dimensions with a query), depth, contact (nothing floats or interpenetrates), camera read (a small low-sample `BLENDER_EEVEE` render from the delivery camera), detail. `BLENDER_WORKBENCH` ignores scene lights, so it proves form only.

A succeeded mutation proves the code ran, not that the scene is right. Render from the delivery camera, retrieve the artifact, look at it, fix the largest visible defect and re-render before calling the work done.

Load the reference the task calls for before that stage:

- `/3d-jutsu/references/scene-building` before any multi-object or whole-scene build.
- `/3d-jutsu/references/composition-modeling` before detailed geometry, hard-surface work or GLB export.
- `/3d-jutsu/references/lookdev-lighting` before materials, textures or lighting beyond the working rig.
- `/3d-jutsu/references/animation-audit` before keyframes, camera motion, loops or turntables.

## Deliver

- Files: `scene_builder_3d_get_glb` for a portable model and `scene_builder_3d_get_blend` for the editable source, only when the user wants them. Procedural shaders and world lighting do not reliably carry into GLB.
- AI image or video from a render: `scene_builder_3d_generate_angles` (image) and `scene_builder_3d_generate_video` (Seedance 2.5 video with the render as its start frame) spend credits and leave the scene unchanged. Use them only when the user asks for an AI image or video from the scene, with an inspected PNG/JPEG render's `operationId` and `artifactId`, then poll `scene_builder_3d_get_generation`. On an uncertain response, reuse the same `requestId` and arguments; never allocate a new one just to retry.
- At each completed scene review or delivery, call `scene_builder_3d_show_scene` once with the exact final `revisionAfter` (or settled `revision` after import), after settlement and visual verification. Do not repeat an unchanged revision. This ends that phase's scene inspection/edit calls; authorized generation and status calls may follow. Later feedback or a verified mismatch may reopen editing; verify and show the corrected revision at its next review boundary. If widgets are unavailable, give the returned `projectUrl`.


## Available references

Read a reference only when needed by calling get_preset_instructions with the exact preset argument below.

- {"preset":"/3d-jutsu/references/composition-modeling"}

- {"preset":"/3d-jutsu/references/lookdev-lighting"}

# Scene Building

Build the scene as an editable visual system, not as a pile of objects or a Python script that merely finishes without errors. Preserve intentional existing work, make decisions at real metre scale, and judge every important choice from the delivery camera.

This guide owns scene-making judgment. The mechanics — project selection, the revision guard, `scene_builder_3d_query_python` for inspection, `scene_builder_3d_run_python` for mutations, `artifacts` for renders, the execution deadline — are in the `/3d-jutsu` entrypoint and are not repeated here. Load `/3d-jutsu/references/composition-modeling`, `/3d-jutsu/references/lookdev-lighting` or `/3d-jutsu/references/animation-audit` with `get_preset_instructions` when the work reaches those stages.

## Establish the scene contract

Before a whole-scene or multi-object build, write a concise Scene Passport in your working notes or reasoning (not a message to the user). Keep it specific enough that later visual checks can pass or fail against it:

```text
SCENE       intent; deliverable; metre scale; render resolution; static or animated
HIERARCHY   semantic collections; parent relationships; protected existing objects
ASSETS      role; route [EXISTING|PROCEDURAL|IMPORTED]; fidelity; dimensions; placement; origin
SHOT        active camera; subject; lens/framing; foreground, midground, background
LOOK        palette; material roles; texture scale; roughness/metallic/relief intent
LIGHTING    focal subject; darkest region; key motivation/direction/softness; fill; reflections
MOTION      fps/range; primary beat; secondary motion; rest pose; loop, if any
ACCEPTANCE  structural, motion, and visual conditions visible in the final deliverable
```

`IMPORTED` assets come in through `scene_builder_3d_import_asset` and nothing else: search the curated catalog with `scene_builder_3d_search_assets` and copy its `importArguments`. This version imports catalog assets only; a model the user attached cannot be imported yet, so say so and offer a catalog or procedural alternative. Each import is one tracked entity, placed with the tool's `transform`; adjust it afterwards with an ordinary mutation rather than re-importing. Do not fetch, decode, or paste model bytes in Python.

Use semantic, unique names that express role, such as `ENV_floor`, `HERO_robot`, `PRP_table`, `CAM_main`, `LGT_key`, and `RIG_turntable`. Decide the fidelity of every camera-visible asset before refinement: hero objects receive full silhouette and material attention; midground objects need a recognizable species/type; background geometry may remain simple when it reads correctly.

## Build from coarse decisions to fine ones

The first mutation lays scaffolding along with the first shapes: the delivery camera (`CAM_main`) at its intended lens and height, and a **working light rig** — modest world ambient, one motivated key (`LGT_key`, Sun or Spot, aimed per the Passport's LIGHTING row), one soft fill (`LGT_fill`, a large-radius Point or Spot). Avoid Area lights: the scene view and GLB export drop them. A dozen lines, no cost; it means every revision the user opens is lit and every render from here on judges form and light together. Do not defer light until the geometry is "ready" — the geometry is never ready before the light that reads it exists.

Then work through these gates in order:

1. **Silhouette:** establish footprint, height, dominant contour, and subject/background separation.
2. **Proportion:** verify dimensions and relative scale numerically in metres — a `scene_builder_3d_query_python` over `obj.dimensions` and bounding boxes is free and settles it.
3. **Depth:** establish foreground, subject, background, overlap, negative space, and visible thickness.
4. **Contact:** remove floating, interpenetration, implausible support, and unusable pivots.
5. **Camera read:** confirm the focal hierarchy and major forms under the working rig — a small, low-sample `BLENDER_EEVEE` render from the delivery camera is fast enough for a blockout and shows form and light together. `BLENDER_WORKBENCH` ignores scene lights; use it for pure-form checks, not for this gate.
6. **Detail:** refine each visible asset only to the fidelity its role and delivery resolution require.

A failed gate stops downstream polish. Fix the largest silhouette, scale, placement, or framing problem before adding topology, materials, or fine detail. Lighting is exempt in one direction only: re-aiming the working rig to follow moved geometry is part of fixing the gate; adding new lighting roles is polish and waits for the gate to pass.

Each gate is one or two mutations, not one giant script: a revision history that reads as a sequence of intentions is also the one where a failure is easy to localize.

## Develop the image, not isolated assets

The working rig exists from the first mutation; grow it alongside the objects it lights rather than in one lighting pass at the end — a fill when the shadow side of the hero arrives, a rim when the background closes in behind it, a practical when the fixture that motivates it is modelled. Lock the primary camera before the final lighting balance. Choose lens and perspective deliberately; extreme focal length is not a repair for wrong geometry. Build materials as a hierarchy of roles rather than independent attractive swatches. Keep the rig's one motivated key, then add fill, separation, practicals, reflection cards, or atmosphere only when each solves a named visual problem.

## Use motion purposefully

Unless the requested deliverable is explicitly static, give the scene at least one readable beat. Prefer one clear primary action and restrained secondary motion, with a stable frame suitable for inspection and thumbnails. Do not make everything move merely to satisfy an animation requirement.

## Prove the scene

Execution success is not visual success. A mutation that returned `succeeded` proves the code ran; it proves nothing about what the scene looks like. Before calling a scene complete:

- inspect structural state: expected objects, transforms, parenting, materials, cameras, and frame range;

# Animation and Scene Audit

Read this guide before animation, camera motion, loops, turntables, constraints, or final approval of an animated scene.

## What the deadline means for animation

Every operation has a service-configured execution deadline (currently about five minutes), and a video render is the work most likely to exceed it: `bpy.ops.render.render(animation=True)` scales with every frame, and a timed-out operation commits nothing. Plan the deliverable around that:

- **Keyframes are cheap; rendering them is not.** Build and key the whole animation in one or two mutations, then prove it with **stills**: `scene.frame_set(n)` followed by a single `write_still=True` render, one or two frames per operation, at the sampled frames the audit below names.
- **An MP4 is a stretch goal, not the default.** Attempt one only when the user explicitly wants video, after the stills pass, with a tiny frame range, low resolution and `BLENDER_WORKBENCH` or low-sample `BLENDER_EEVEE`. If it times out, say so and deliver the stills plus the `.blend` (`scene_builder_3d_get_blend`) so the user can render locally — do not burn a dozen operations shaving samples.
- A rendered MP4 shows the authored animation. A Seedance video from `scene_builder_3d_generate_video` is a paid AI generation from one render, not a render of the keyed motion; use it only when the user asks for AI video.
- The `.blend` export carries the animation intact. For many users that, not a video file, is the actual deliverable.

## Plan readable motion

Define fps, frame range, duration, rest pose, beat structure, motion carrier, and loop boundary before keying. A useful default beat is anticipation, action, and settle. Prefer one clear primary action, restrained secondary responses, and a stable frame suitable for inspection and thumbnails.

When the brief does not prescribe motion:

- product or prop: slow turntable or camera orbit that settles on the hero angle;
- environment: subtle camera drift plus a restrained practical-light change;
- rigged character or creature: small idle breathing or weight shift;
- abstract subject: one focal transformation with a small secondary response.

Do not invent character acting, destructive simulation, or a camera that never rests when subtle motion satisfies the deliverable.

## Build semantic animation

- Key rigs and named controls rather than many unrelated child transforms.
- Key only properties that actually change.
- Choose interpolation deliberately: Bezier for shaped organic timing, linear for constant rates, constant for switches.
- Choose Euler or quaternion rotation deliberately and test for flips.
- Remember that object and object-data animation are separate: camera lens, focus, and clipping belong to camera data, not the camera object's transform curves.
- Make simulations deterministic enough that audited frames reproduce — and remember that a simulation bake is execution time you do not have; prefer keyed motion.

Constraint and contact checks should prove the physical relationship that matters. A spinning child with residual positional offset can orbit away from its mount. Copy only the steering component needed and in the correct control space. For rolling contact, rotation per distance is `distance / radius`; verify the ground contact residual rather than the relationship to a moving parent.

For planted supports on uneven terrain, sample multiple support points. Mean gap supplies height correction; left/right and front/back differences supply roll and pitch. Ease the correction into and out of the shot so it does not pop.

Symmetric fast rotors can appear to reverse when their per-frame step approaches a multiple of the symmetry sector. Adjust angular step and judge motion blur from renders; numeric state does not prove the final rotational read.

Use constant interpolation for visibility switches. Keep constraint targets evaluable even when hidden from final render, and ensure objects not needed in a shot do not continue blocking cameras or affecting lighting.

## Structural audit

One `scene_builder_3d_query_python` can check all of this against the Scene Passport:

- every expected semantic object exists exactly once;
- dimensions, transforms, origins, parents, collections, and visibility are correct;
- active camera, resolution, render engine, fps, and full frame range match the deliverable;
- the final frame includes the final marker and last key;
- material slots and texture references resolve;
- no stray defaults, duplicate suffixes, orphan proxies, or hidden failures remain;
- hero/export meshes have appropriate normals, closure, and density.

## Motion audit

Inspect at least first/rest, departure, fastest or largest change, settle, final, and the loop seam. At each sample verify framing, collision/intersection, surface contact, visibility, constraints, shading continuity, and motion direction.

Render those frames as stills, retrieve them with `scene_builder_3d_get_artifact`, and look at them with this client's image capability. Numeric evaluation — `matrix_world` at each sampled frame — proves an object is where you keyed it and is in frame; it cannot prove the motion reads. Motion fails when expected properties have no keys, promised motion is imperceptible, objects teleport, rotations flip, the camera loses the subject, constraints jump, or the loop has a visible seam. A single still cannot pass an animation audit; a rest frame plus peak plus final is the minimum.

## Visual audit

View evidence from the delivery camera at delivery scale. Check:

- silhouette and focal hierarchy;
- contact, scale cues, and depth separation;
- texture scale and material/reflection readability;
- highlight and shadow detail without clipping or crushed form;
- coherence between imported and locally built assets;
- framing throughout motion;
- whether any camera-visible asset still reads as an unresolved primitive despite requiring higher fidelity.

Downsampled previews can erase features only a few pixels wide. Inspect critical regions at 1:1 before concluding that detail is absent. Numeric projections can prove that an object is in frame, but cannot prove that it looks like the intended subject.

## Repair and finish

Fix the largest concrete failure first: scale, framing, contact, silhouette, motion, lighting, then secondary detail. Rerun the affected audit rather than polishing unrelated areas. If visual evidence is unavailable, report the visual check as blocked.

Keep modifiers, rigs, materials, and semantic parts editable unless the deliverable explicitly requires destructive application. Restore the intended camera and a useful rest frame. Report material limitations, remaining continuity risks, and any checks that could not be viewed.

아래 장면 순서대로 숏폼 프리비즈를 만들어 주세요.

제목: 수능응원

개요: 밝은 교실 안에서 남성 2명, 여성 1명의 혼성 아이돌 그룹이 카메라를 바라보며 나란히 서 있다.

교실에는 칠판, 책상, 의자, 교탁, 벽면 안내문 등 실제 수능 시험을 앞둔 교실 분위기가 자연스럽게 보인다.
전체적으로 따뜻하고 단정한 분위기이며, 수험생 응원 현장 느낌이 난다.

세 멤버가 밝게 웃으며 손을 흔들고 인사한다.

남성 1: "수험생 여러분, 지금까지 정말 고생 많았어요!"
여성: "열심히 준비한 만큼 좋은 결과가 있길 바라요!"
남성 2: "긴장하지 말고 여러분 자신을 믿으세요!"

마지막으로 세 멤버가 동시에 주먹을 들어 올리며
"수능 대박! 파이팅!"이라고 힘차게 외친 뒤 손하트를 만든다.

밝고 활기찬 분위기, 자연스러운 표정과 제스처,
정확한 한국어 립싱크, 정면 상반신 중심 촬영.

1. 따뜻한 교실 속 인사
밝고 따뜻한 햇살이 들어오는 교실 안, 칠판과 책상이 놓인 배경 앞에 남성 2명과 여성 1명으로 구성된 혼성 아이돌 그룹이 정면을 바라보며 나란히 서서 카메라를 향해 환하게 웃으며 손을 흔든다. 정면 상반신을 중심으로 촬영하며, 활기찬 교실의 소음과 함께 멤버들의 밝은 인사 소리가 들린다.

2. 멤버들의 진심 어린 응원
카메라를 응시하는 멤버들의 얼굴이 정면으로 강조되며, 남성 1이 다정한 미소로 "수험생 여러분, 지금까지 정말 고생 많았어요!"라고 말하고 이어 여성이 "열심히 준비한 만큼 좋은 결과가 있길 바라요!"라고 진심을 담아 말하며, 남성 2가 "긴장하지 말고 여러분 자신을 믿으세요!"라고 격려하며 자연스러운 입 모양과 표정을 보여준다.

3. 수능 대박 파이팅
세 멤버가 한목소리로 "수능 대박! 파이팅!"이라고 힘차게 외치며 동시에 주먹을 불끈 들어 올리고, 이어서 카메라를 향해 사랑스러운 손하트를 만들며 밝고 에너제틱하게 마무리한다. 정면 상반신 중심의 구도에서 멤버들의 역동적인 움직임과 활기찬 함성 소리가 조화롭게 울려 퍼진다.
